claim: Naive B cells co-express two BCR isotypes, IgM and IgD, with identical antigen-binding domains but distinct constant regions.
source: Naive B cells co-express two BCR isotypes, IgM and IgD, with identical antigen-binding domains but distinct constant regions.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about B cell receptor structure.

claim: IgM but not IgD is downregulated on autoreactive B cells.
source: IgM but not IgD is downregulated on autoreactive B cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by prior published work and data presented in the manuscript.

claim: IgD is less sensitive than IgM to endogenous antigen in vivo despite signaling strongly in vitro.
source: Despite signaling strongly in vitro, IgD is less sensitive than IgM to endogenous antigen in vivo and developmental fate decisions are skewed accordingly.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: IgD-only Lyn−/− B cells cannot generate autoantibodies and short-lived plasma cells (SLPCs) in vivo.
source: IgD-only Lyn−/− B cells cannot generate autoantibodies and short-lived plasma cells (SLPCs) in vivo, a fate thought to be driven by intense BCR signaling induced by endogenous antigens.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data in the manuscript.

claim: IgD-only B cells generate normal germinal center, but impaired IgG1+ SLPC responses to T-dependent immunization.
source: Similarly, IgD-only B cells generate normal germinal center, but impaired IgG1+ SLPC responses to T-dependent immunization.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by immunization data in the manuscript.

claim: Early in development, B cells randomly rearrange their immunoglobulin genes through VDJ recombination.
source: Early in development, B cells randomly rearrange their immunoglobulin genes through VDJ recombination and encounter a series of tolerance checkpoints that serve to remove autoreactive B cell receptors (BCRs) from the repertoire.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about B cell development.

claim: Strongly autoreactive immature B cells rearrange additional light chains to 'edit' their autoreactivity.
source: Strongly autoreactive immature B cells rearrange additional light chains to 'edit' their autoreactivity, and they ultimately undergo deletion if this is unsuccessful (Shlomchik, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The mature follicular (Fo) B cell compartment retains cells reactive towards endogenous antigens despite stringent counter-selection of autoreactivity.
source: Yet, despite stringent counter-selection of autoreactivity, the mature follicular (Fo) B cell compartment retains cells reactive towards endogenous antigens (Wardemann et al., 2003; Zikherman et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Nur77-eGFP expression in naïve B cells is proportional to strength of antigenic stimulation and consequently to autoreactivity.
source: We showed that Nur77-eGFP expression in naïve B cells is proportional to strength of antigenic stimulation and consequently to autoreactivity (Zikherman et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work and data in Figure 1A.

claim: The most prominent characteristic of GFPhi reporter B cells is decreased surface IgM BCR relative to GFPlo cells.
source: The most prominent characteristic of GFPhi reporter B cells is decreased surface IgM BCR relative to GFPlo cells.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Goodnow and colleagues first suggested that IgM downregulation may mark autoreactive B cells in the normal mature repertoire.
source: Goodnow and colleagues first suggested that IgM downregulation may mark autoreactive B cells in the normal mature repertoire shortly after they reported selective downregulation of IgM in the IgHEL (hen egg lysozyme) BCR Tg/soluble HEL Tg model system of B cell autoreactivity (Goodnow et al., 1988; Goodnow et al., 1989).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Multiple studies in mice and humans have identified naturally occurring IgD+IgMlo cells as autoreactive and 'anergic' or functionally unresponsive.
source: Indeed, multiple studies in mice and humans have identified naturally occurring IgD+IgMlo cells as autoreactive and 'anergic' or functionally unresponsive (Duty et al., 2009; Kirchenbaum et al., 2014; Quách et al., 2011; Zikherman et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior published work.

claim: IgM and IgD are splice isoforms of a common precursor heavy chain mRNA.
source: IgM and IgD are splice isoforms of a common precursor heavy chain mRNA (Moore et al., 1981).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Both IgM and IgD BCR isotypes contain the same antigen-binding domain, as well as identical 3-amino acid cytoplasmic tails.
source: While they differ in their Fc domains, both BCR isotypes contain the same antigen-binding domain, as well as identical 3-amino acid cytoplasmic tails, and they pair with Igα/β in order to initiate the canonical BCR signaling cascade (Blum et al., 1993; Radaev et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: IgM expression begins as soon as heavy and light chains recombine early in B cell development, and persists until class switch recombination occurs following B cell activation.
source: IgM expression begins as soon as heavy and light chains recombine early in B cell development, and persists until class switch recombination occurs following B cell activation (Chen and Cerutti, 2010).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: IgD is uniquely co-expressed with IgM during a narrow developmental window on late transitional and mature naïve Fo B cells as a result of alternate splicing regulated by the zinc-finger protein ZFP318.
source: IgD is uniquely co-expressed with IgM during a narrow developmental window on late transitional and mature naïve Fo B cells as a result of alternate splicing regulated by the zinc-finger protein ZFP318 (Enders et al., 2014; Pioli et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Initial characterization of IgM- and IgD-deficient mice revealed only mild phenotypes and substantial redundancy.
source: Initial characterization of IgM- and IgD-deficient mice revealed only mild phenotypes and substantial redundancy; each isotype could mediate B cell development, initiate antibody responses to T-dependent and -independent immunization, and induce normal levels of steady-state serum IgG (Lutz et al., 1998; Nitschke et al., 1993; Roes and Rajewsky, 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: IgD has a much longer, flexible hinge region linking its Fab and Fc regions than IgM does.
source: IgM and IgD differ structurally; IgD has a much longer, flexible hinge region linking its Fab and Fc regions than IgM does (Chen and Cerutti, 2010).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: A short and inflexible hinge confers upon IgM the unique capacity to signal in response to monovalent antigens, while both isotypes can respond to multivalent antigens.
source: Recently, Ubelhart, Jumaa, and colleagues demonstrated that a short and inflexible hinge confers upon IgM the unique capacity to signal in response to monovalent antigens, while both isotypes can respond to multivalent antigens (Übelhart et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: IgHEL Tg splenic B cells expressing either the IgD or IgM BCR exclusively can mobilize calcium in response to soluble HEL antigen in vitro.
source: However, the Goodnow lab subsequently showed that IgHEL Tg splenic B cells expressing either the IgD or IgM BCR exclusively could mobilize calcium in response to soluble HEL antigen in vitro, and each isotype can mediate a common gene expression program characteristic of anergy in vivo (Sabouri et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: 5–10% of circulating naïve B cells in healthy humans express the well-characterized unmutated and autoreactive human heavy chain V-segment IGHV4-34.
source: For example, 5–10% of circulating naïve B cells in healthy humans express the well-characterized unmutated and autoreactive human heavy chain V-segment IGHV4-34, and these cells exhibit anergy, selective IgM downregulation, and recognize cell-surface antigens on erythrocytes and B cells in vivo (Quách et al., 2011; Reed et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: IGHV4-34 expressing B cells exhibit anergy, selective IgM downregulation, and recognize cell-surface antigens on erythrocytes and B cells in vivo.
source: For example, 5–10% of circulating naïve B cells in healthy humans express the well-characterized unmutated and autoreactive human heavy chain V-segment IGHV4-34, and these cells exhibit anergy, selective IgM downregulation, and recognize cell-surface antigens on erythrocytes and B cells in vivo (Quách et al., 2011; Reed et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Marginal zone (MZ) and B1a cells that express IgD but lack IgM induce less Nur77-eGFP than WT.
source: Indeed, marginal zone (MZ) and B1a cells that express IgD but lack IgM induce less Nur77-eGFP than WT, and this is not attributable to repertoire differences.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: IgD drives a pattern of development consistent with reduced endogenous antigen recognition, favoring MZ B cell fate and disfavoring B1a cell fate.
source: We show that IgD drives a pattern of development consistent with reduced endogenous antigen recognition, favoring MZ B cell fate and disfavoring B1a cell fate.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: IgD alone is less efficient than IgM at driving SLPC expansion in response to endogenous antigens.
source: Similarly, IgD alone is less efficient than IgM at driving SLPC expansion in response to endogenous antigens, a process that requires robust BCR signaling.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: IgD is sufficient for germinal center (GC) B cell differentiation.
source: However, IgD is sufficient for germinal center (GC) B cell differentiation.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figures 5 and 7.

claim: Antigen recognition is both necessary and sufficient for Nur77-eGFP reporter expression by B cells in vivo.
source: We previously showed that antigen recognition was both necessary and sufficient for Nur77-eGFP reporter expression by B cells in vivo (Figure 1A)(Zikherman et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work and data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Under steady-state conditions in vivo, the Nur77-eGFP reporter does not reflect signaling through other receptors expressed in B cells.
source: Conversely, under steady-state conditions in vivo, the Nur77-eGFP reporter does not reflect signaling through other receptors expressed in B cells; indeed, loss of either CD40, or TLR3, 7, and 9 signaling has no effect on reporter expression in B cells in vivo (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: BAFF, IL-4, and CXCR4-dependent signaling cannot regulate Nur77-eGFP reporter expression in vitro.
source: Moreover, neither BAFF, nor IL-4, nor CXCR4-dependent signaling can regulate reporter expression in vitro (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–C) (Zikherman et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–C and a citation.

claim: Nur77 expression in naïve B cells under steady state conditions is not regulated by microbial stimulation of pattern recognition receptors in germ-free versus conventional specific-pathogen-free conditions.
source: To further confirm that Nur77 expression in naïve B cells under steady state conditions is not regulated by microbial stimulation of pattern recognition receptors (e.g. TLRs 1, 2, 4, 6, and the TLR-4-like molecule RP105), we studied mice raised under either germ-free conditions or conventional specific-pathogen-free conditions. We observed no induction of endogenous Nur77 protein in splenic B cells or endogenous Nr4a1 transcript in splenocytes in the presence of commensal flora (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D,E.

claim: MyD88-deficient and MyD88-sufficient splenocytes and peritoneal B1a cells express comparable amounts of endogenous Nr4a1 transcript and protein respectively under steady state conditions.
source: Moreover, MyD88-deficient and MyD88-sufficient splenocytes and peritoneal B1a cells express comparable amounts of endogenous Nr4a1 transcript and protein respectively under steady state conditions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F,G.

claim: Nur77-eGFP expression in B cells under steady-state conditions in vivo is a specific readout of antigen-dependent signaling through the BCR.
source: Taken together, these data demonstrate that Nur77-eGFP expression in B cells under steady-state conditions in vivo is a specific readout of antigen-dependent signaling through the BCR (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data summarized in Table 1 and multiple figures.

claim: Surface IgM, but not IgD, expression is inversely correlated with endogenous antigen recognition and GFP expression across a diverse repertoire of mature naïve follicular (Fo) B cells.
source: Surface IgM, but not IgD, expression is inversely correlated with endogenous antigen recognition and GFP expression across a diverse repertoire of mature naïve follicular (Fo) B cells, such that B cells reactive to endogenous antigens express high levels of IgD and low levels of IgM on their surface (Figure 1B) (Zikherman et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B and a citation to prior work.

claim: The variation in surface IgM expression across the B cell repertoire spans a 100-fold range.
source: The variation in surface IgM expression across the B cell repertoire is profound, spanning a 100-fold range.
evidence: This is an observation from data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: IgD is expressed at high and invariant levels in all WT naïve Fo B cells.
source: However, because IgD is expressed at high and invariant levels in all WT naïve Fo B cells, total surface BCR, unlike IgM, has little dynamic range across the WT repertoire (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is an observation from data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: IgM is still downregulated on IgD−/− GFPhi Fo B cells, but the dynamic range of IgM expression is highly restricted relative to the broad range observed on WT cells.
source: We observed that IgM is still downregulated on IgD−/− GFPhi Fo B cells, but the dynamic range of IgM expression is highly restricted relative to the broad range observed on WT cells (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: IgM down-modulation on GFPhi reporter B cells largely accounts for impaired signaling through IgM.
source: We previously showed that IgM down-modulation on GFPhi reporter B cells largely accounts for impaired signaling through IgM (Figure 1C) (Zikherman et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1C and a citation to prior work.

claim: The narrow dynamic range of IgM on IgD-deficient cells renders reporter B cells unable to fine-tune signaling through the IgM BCR across the GFP repertoire.
source: However, the narrow dynamic range of IgM on IgD-deficient cells renders reporter B cells unable to fine-tune signaling through the IgM BCR across the GFP repertoire (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: IgD-mediated signaling is not altered across the GFP repertoire in the presence or absence of IgM.
source: Furthermore, IgD-mediated signaling is not altered across the GFP repertoire in the presence or absence of IgM (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Reduced responsiveness of GFPhi B cells is most profound in B cells that express the IgM isotype in the presence of IgD.
source: As a result, reduced responsiveness of GFPhi B cells is most profound in B cells that express the IgM isotype in the presence of IgD.
evidence: This is an inference from data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: IgD expression may be necessary to establish and/or maintain a broad and functionally dynamic range of surface IgM expression across the B cell repertoire.
source: This suggests that IgD expression may be necessary to establish and/or maintain a broad and functionally dynamic range of surface IgM expression across the B cell repertoire.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data.

claim: IgD expression is consistent with a previously proposed survival function for the IgD BCR.
source: This is consistent with a previously proposed survival function for the IgD BCR (Roes and Rajewsky, 1993; Sabouri et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Deletion of either the IgM or the IgD BCR isotype results in compensatory upregulation of the remaining isotype.
source: Deletion of either the IgM or the IgD BCR isotype results in compensatory upregulation of the remaining isotype.
evidence: This is an observation supported by data in Figure 1D.

claim: Compensatory upregulation of BCR isotypes may be due in part to a change in competition for pairing with Igα/β heterodimers, which is essential for trafficking of IgM to the cell surface.
source: This may be due in part to a change in competition for pairing with Igα/β heterodimers, which is essential for trafficking of IgM to the cell surface (Hombach et al., 1990; Sabouri et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by citations to prior work.

claim: IgM−/− B cells express about twice as much surface BCR as IgD−/− B cells, as measured by surface anti-light chain staining.
source: IgM−/− B cells express about twice as much surface BCR as IgD−/− B cells, as measured by surface anti-light chain staining (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2B–E).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2B–E.

claim: Distribution of Nur77-eGFP expression across the naïve B cell repertoire is nearly identical in IgM−/− and IgD−/− Fo B cells.
source: Nevertheless, distribution of Nur77-eGFP expression across the naïve B cell repertoire is nearly identical in IgM−/− and IgD−/− Fo B cells (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: At every level of Nur77-eGFP, cells that express IgD alone require more surface BCR to drive an equivalent amount of GFP compared to cells that express IgM alone.
source: Further, at every level of Nur77-eGFP, cells that express IgD alone require more surface BCR to drive an equivalent amount of GFP compared to cells that express IgM alone (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: On a per-receptor basis, IgD BCR may be less efficient at inducing Nur77-eGFP in response to endogenous antigens.
source: This suggests that on a per-receptor basis, IgD BCR may be less efficient at inducing Nur77-eGFP in response to endogenous antigens.
evidence: This is an inference from data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Differential Nur77-eGFP induction by IgM and IgD is not attributable to differential dependence upon IgM or IgD expression for signaling via CXCR4 or downstream of canonical TLR ligands.
source: Importantly, this is not attributable to differential dependence upon IgM or IgD expression for signaling via CXCR4 or downstream of canonical TLR ligands (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: BCR ligation in IgD-only B cells induced equivalent amounts of Erk phosphorylation relative to IgM-only B cells.
source: BCR ligation in IgD-only B cells induced equivalent amounts of Erk phosphorylation relative to IgM-only B cells (Figure 2A), and there were no gross differences in pErk kinetics (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: IgD-only cells induced more robust intracellular calcium increase and S6 phosphorylation than IgM-only cells.
source: Additionally, IgD-only cells induced more robust intracellular calcium increase and S6 phosphorylation than IgM-only cells (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Differential signaling between IgM-only and IgD-only B cells was not due to differential effects of the Fc portion of the stimulatory antibody.
source: This was not due to differential effects of the Fc portion of the stimulatory antibody on IgM-only and IgD-only B cells as anti-Igκ-F(ab')2 and anti-Igκ stimulation produced identical signaling (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: IgD-only B cells induce significantly more CD86 and Nur77-eGFP induction than IgM-only B cells after 18 hr of anti-Igκ stimulation in vitro.
source: As a result, we observe significantly more CD86 and Nur77-eGFP induction in IgD-only B cells after 18 hr of anti-Igκ stimulation in vitro (Figure 2D–F).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 2D–F.

claim: IgD-only cells induced less Nur77-eGFP and MHC-II upregulation when cultured in the absence of exogenous stimulus.
source: However, IgD-only cells induced less Nur77-eGFP and MHC-II upregulation when cultured in the absence of exogenous stimulus (Figure 2G and H).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 2G and H.

claim: Residual endogenous antigens occupying the IgD BCR are less efficient at inducing signaling ex vivo.
source: This discrepancy suggests that despite increased receptor expression and efficient coupling to downstream signaling machinery, residual endogenous antigens occupying the IgD BCR are less efficient at inducing signaling ex vivo.
evidence: This is an inference from data shown in Figure 2G and H.

claim: Basal calcium analyzed immediately ex vivo is depressed in cells that express only IgD.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, basal calcium analyzed immediately ex vivo is depressed in cells that express only IgD (Figure 2I).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: While signal transduction downstream of the IgD BCR is robust in vitro, IgD responds less efficiently than IgM to the relevant antigens it encounters in vivo.
source: These data suggest that while signal transduction downstream of the IgD BCR is robust in vitro, IgD responds less efficiently than IgM to the relevant antigens it encounters in vivo.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from data in Figure 2.

claim: IgD-only marginal zone (MZ) and B1a cells expressed significantly less Nur77-eGFP than WT cells despite higher levels of surface BCR.
source: In contrast to Fo B cells, IgD-only marginal zone (MZ) and B1a cells expressed significantly less Nur77-eGFP than WT cells despite higher levels of surface BCR (Figure 3A, Figure 1—figure supplement 2B–E).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 1—figure supplement 2B–E.

claim: A large difference in GFP exists even among B1a cells with a common specificity for phosphatidylcholine (PtC).
source: We found a large difference in GFP even among B1a cells with a common specificity, and this occurs in spite of high surface PtC binding in IgD-only B1a cells (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: In BAFF Tg mice, IgD-only MZ cells expressed much less GFP than those expressing IgM alone.
source: In BAFF Tg mice, IgD-only MZ cells expressed much less GFP than those expressing IgM alone (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 3D and E.

claim: Differences in surface receptor levels between IgD-only and IgM-only MZ cells do not explain GFP differences on the BAFF Tg genetic background.
source: This was not explained by differences in surface receptor levels between these populations as they are comparable on this genetic background (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: IgD-only cells with low GFP and IgM-only cells with high GFP appear to be preferentially rescued in mice with excess BAFF.
source: Indeed, IgD-only cells with low GFP and IgM-only cells with high GFP appear to be preferentially rescued in mice with excess BAFF, suggesting that distinct BCR repertoires, far from accounting for GFP differences between IgM-only and IgD-only MZ B cells, actually obscure these differences.
evidence: This is an inference from data shown in Figure 3D and E.

claim: The Nur77-eGFP difference in the MZ and B1a compartments is cell intrinsic and not a consequence of the presence or absence of serum IgM.
source: We exploited this property to confirm that the Nur77-eGFP difference in the MZ and B1a compartments is cell intrinsic and not a consequence of the presence or absence of serum IgM (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Differences in MZ GFP are due to BCR isotype and not VDJ locus.
source: We took this approach to confirm that differences in MZ GFP were due to BCR isotype and not VDJ locus (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Generation of the B1a compartment requires endogenous antigen recognition and strong BCR signaling.
source: Generation of the B1a compartment requires endogenous antigen recognition and strong BCR signaling, while the opposite is true for MZ B cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) (Cariappa and Pillai, 2002; Casola et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: B1a cells are modestly reduced in IgM-deficient mice, while MZ B cells are modestly increased.
source: Indeed, B1a cells are modestly reduced in IgM-deficient mice, while MZ B cells are modestly increased (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–C.

claim: IgD-only cells are virtually excluded from the B1a compartment in a competitive setting.
source: Although IgD-only B cells can partially populate the B1a compartment in the absence of competition (Lutz et al., 1998; Übelhart et al., 2015), IgD-only cells are virtually excluded from this compartment in a competitive setting (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 4B and citations to prior work.

claim: IgD-only B cells preferentially populate the MZ B cell compartment in competition with IgM-only B cells.
source: In contrast, IgD-only B cells preferentially populate the MZ B cell compartment in competition with IgM-only B cells (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Differences in signaling between IgD-only and IgM-only B cells are consistent with a signal strength model of B1a/MZ B cell development.
source: These data are consistent with a signal strength model of B1a/MZ B cell development (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), and this suggests that in vivo signaling, antigen recognition, or both are reduced in IgD-only B cells.
evidence: This is an interpretation of data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Skewed development of B cell lineages is primarily attributable to lack of IgM expression on IgD-only cells rather than lack of IgD expression on IgM-only cells.
source: We conclude that skewing of MZ and B1a fates is primarily attributable to lack of IgM expression on IgD-only cells rather than lack of IgD expression on IgM-only cells because we observe little skewing in IgD+/− mice (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from data shown in Figure 4C–E.

claim: The competitive advantage of IgD-only cells in the marginal zone niche is reduced by BAFF over-expression.
source: Further, the competitive advantage of IgD-only cells in the marginal zone niche is reduced by BAFF over-expression, consistent with loosening of competitive selection pressures (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: IgM-only B cells exhibit a disadvantage in the mature Fo compartment relative to IgD-only B cells.
source: IgM-only B cells exhibit a disadvantage in the mature Fo compartment relative to IgD-only B cells (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Absence of IgD rather than excess IgM expression accounts for some of the disadvantage of IgM-only B cells in the Fo compartment.
source: We find that absence of IgD rather than excess IgM expression accounts for some of this disadvantage as WT and IgD-only cells compete equally well in this compartment (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The disadvantage for Fo B cells lacking IgD may reflect impaired positive selection or survival in absence of IgD.
source: This may reflect impaired positive selection or survival in absence of IgD.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data.

claim: A disadvantage for Fo B cells lacking IgD was observed in IgD+/− mice previously.
source: Indeed, similar to our observations, a disadvantage for Fo B cells lacking IgD was observed in IgD+/− mice previously (Roes and Rajewsky, 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: The developmental fates of IgM-only and IgD-only cells are due to BCR isotype and not VDJ locus.
source: As with differences in Nur77-eGFP expression, we confirmed that the developmental fates of IgM-only and IgD-only cells were due to BCR isotype and not VDJ locus (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Lyn−/− mice develop a spontaneous lupus-like disease characterized by anti-DNA antibodies and nephritis on the C57BL/6 genetic background.
source: Lyn−/− mice consequently develop a spontaneous lupus-like disease characterized by anti-DNA antibodies and nephritis on the C57BL/6 genetic background (Chan et al., 1997; Hibbs et al., 1995; Nishizumi et al., 1995).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Both B-cell-specific MyD88 expression and T cells are essential for IgG2a/c anti-dsDNA autoantibody production in Lyn−/− mice.
source: It has been shown that both B-cell-specific MyD88 expression and T cells are essential for IgG2a/c anti-dsDNA autoantibody production in Lyn−/− mice, and conditional deletion of Lyn in B cells is sufficient for autoimmunity (Hua et al., 2014; Lamagna et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Secreted natural IgM is thought to play important homeostatic functions that repress autoimmunity, particularly clearance of dead cell debris.
source: Secreted natural IgM is thought to play important homeostatic functions that repress autoimmunity, particularly clearance of dead cell debris (Boes et al., 2000; Manson et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Precursor Fo B cells are present at roughly equal ratios from WT and IgM-only or IgD-only loci in IgM+/− Lyn−/− and IgD+/− Lyn−/− mice.
source: Importantly, precursor Fo B cells are present at roughly equal ratios from WT and IgM-only or IgD-only loci in these mice, and this is unaffected by VDJ background (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: Lyn−/− B cells expressing either IgM or IgD alone exhibit enhanced BCR signaling in vitro relative to Lyn+/+ B cells.
source: Moreover, Lyn−/− B cells expressing either IgM or IgD alone exhibit enhanced BCR signaling in vitro relative to Lyn+/+ B cells, suggesting that neither isotype is uniquely coupled to ITIM-containing receptors (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–B.

claim: Polyclonal B cell activation in Lyn−/− mice precedes and is genetically separable from autoantibody production.
source: Polyclonal B cell activation in Lyn−/− mice precedes and is genetically separable from autoantibody production; it is driven by B cell-intrinsic loss of Lyn, is thought to result from enhanced BCR signaling, and is independent of MyD88 expression (Hua et al., 2014; Lamagna et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Lyn−/− reporter B cells have elevated Nur77-eGFP expression consistent with enhanced BCR signal transduction in vivo.
source: Indeed, Lyn−/− reporter B cells have elevated Nur77-eGFP expression consistent with enhanced BCR signal transduction in vivo (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Neither CD86 nor CD69 upregulation were significantly different on WT and IgD-only B cells in the absence of Lyn.
source: We had expected that activation of IgD-only Lyn−/− B cells might be impaired due to reduced sensing of endogenous antigens, but neither CD86 nor CD69 upregulation were significantly different on WT and IgD-only B cells in the absence of Lyn (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Both IgD and IgM BCRs can provide sufficient signals to drive polyclonal activation by endogenous antigens.
source: This implies that both BCRs can provide sufficient signals to drive polyclonal activation by endogenous antigens.
evidence: This is an inference from data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Both IgD-only and IgM-only cells in Lyn-deficient mice made comparable contributions to the GC compartment in competition with wild type B cells.
source: We found that both IgD-only and IgM-only cells in Lyn-deficient mice made comparable contributions to the GC compartment in competition with wild type B cells, independent of VDJ background (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 3B–C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 3B–C.

claim: Endogenous antigen sensing by IgD, while normally dampened, is sufficient to drive both polyclonal activation and GC differentiation on the Lyn−/− background.
source: We propose that endogenous antigen sensing by IgD, while normally dampened, is sufficient to drive both polyclonal activation and GC differentiation on the Lyn−/− background.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from data in Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: Antigen capture by IgD and presentation on MHC-II is robust enough to recruit adequate T cell help to support polyclonal activation and GC differentiation.
source: This further implies that antigen capture by IgD and presentation on MHC-II is robust enough to recruit adequate T cell help to support these cell fates.
evidence: This is an inference from data in Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: B cells expressing IgM (of either IgH locus) generated IgG2a/c anti-dsDNA, while IgD-only B cells were relatively protected from generating anti-dsDNA antibodies.
source: While B cells expressing IgM (of either IgH locus) generated IgG2a/c anti-dsDNA, IgD-only B cells were relatively protected from generating anti-dsDNA antibodies, even at late time points (Figure 5C–G, Figure 5—figure supplement 3D–E).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 5C–G and Figure 5—figure supplement 3D–E.

claim: The protection of IgD-only B cells from generating anti-dsDNA antibodies is attributable to BCR isotype and not VDJ locus.
source: Importantly, this is attributable to BCR isotype and not VDJ locus (Figure 5—figure supplement 3D–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3D–E.

claim: Anti-dsDNA antibody titers fluctuated substantially over time in Lyn−/− mice, in some cases dropping markedly over a four-week period.
source: We noted that anti-dsDNA antibody titers fluctuated substantially over time in Lyn−/− mice, in some cases dropping markedly over a four-week period (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: This is an observation from data shown in Figure 5C and D.

claim: Anti-dsDNA IgG autoantibodies in patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) fluctuate over time and correlate with disease flares.
source: Anti-dsDNA IgG autoantibodies in patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) similarly fluctuate over time – in contrast to other anti-nuclear specificities - and correlate with disease flares (Liu et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: Unmutated germline BCRs from naïve B cells are recruited directly into the circulating plasmablast compartment during SLE flares.
source: Furthermore, unmutated germline BCRs from naïve B cells are recruited directly into the circulating plasmablast compartment during SLE flares (Tipton et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: Anti-dsDNA antibodies in mice and humans are secreted at least in part by SLPCs emerging from an extra-follicular immune response, rather than long-lived plasma cells (LLPCs) that originate in GCs.
source: Taken together, this suggests that anti-dsDNA antibodies in mice and humans are secreted at least in part by SLPCs emerging from an extra-follicular immune response, rather than long-lived plasma cells (LLPCs) that originate in GCs.
evidence: This is an inference from data and cited literature.

claim: In the absence of Lyn, the IgD BCR is sufficient to mediate B cell activation and GC entry, but the IgM BCR is essential to produce dsDNA-specific SLPCs.
source: Our data suggests that, in the absence of Lyn, the IgD BCR is sufficient to mediate B cell activation and GC entry, but the IgM BCR is essential to produce dsDNA-specific SLPCs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from data in Figure 5.

claim: Lyn−/− mice exhibit a massive expansion of the splenic IgM plasma cell compartment that corresponds to a roughly 10-fold increase in serum IgM.
source: In addition to stochastic generation of autoantibodies over time, Lyn−/− mice exhibit a massive expansion of the splenic IgM plasma cell compartment that corresponds to a roughly 10-fold increase in serum IgM (Hibbs et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: Elevated serum IgM in Lyn−/− mice arises from the Fo B2 compartment.
source: While natural IgM is thought to be secreted by B1a-derived plasma cells (Baumgarth, 2011), elevated serum IgM in Lyn−/− mice arises from the Fo B2 compartment since Lyn−/− mice lack MZ B cells, and bone marrow chimeras lacking the B1a compartment reconstitute the hyper-IgM secretion phenotype (Luo et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: BCR signaling is prominently enhanced in Lyn−/− B2 B cells but markedly dampened in Lyn−/− B1a cells.
source: Moreover, while BCR signaling is prominently enhanced in Lyn−/− B2 B cells, it is markedly dampened in Lyn−/− B1a cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A) (Skrzypczynska et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and a citation.

claim: IgM plasma cell expansion in Lyn−/− mice develops in mice as young as 7–10 weeks of age with 100% penetrance, is B-cell intrinsic, and is not dependent upon MyD88 expression.
source: IgM plasma cell expansion is temporally and genetically separable from autoimmunity in Lyn−/− mice; this phenotype develops in mice as young as 7–10 weeks of age with 100% penetrance, is B-cell intrinsic, and is not dependent upon MyD88 expression (Hua et al., 2014; Infantino et al., 2014; Lamagna et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: A pathway involving Btk, Ets1, and Blimp-1 is thought to drive IgM plasma cell expansion in Lyn−/− mice.
source: A pathway involving Btk, Ets1, and Blimp-1 is thought to drive this phenotype.
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior work.

claim: Ets1 inhibits plasma cell differentiation in part by antagonizing the key transcriptional regulator of plasma cell fate, Blimp-1.
source: Ets1 inhibits plasma cell differentiation in part by antagonizing the key transcriptional regulator of plasma cell fate, Blimp-1 (John et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: Mice deficient for Ets1 display IgM plasma cell expansion.
source: Mice deficient for Ets1 display IgM plasma cell expansion, Ets1 levels are reduced in Lyn−/− mice, and restoration of Ets1 expression normalizes IgM plasma cell numbers (Luo et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: Reducing levels of Btk is sufficient to suppress IgM plasma cell expansion in Lyn−/− mice, and Ets1 levels are concomitantly restored to normal levels in Btklo Lyn−/− mice.
source: Furthermore, reducing levels of Btk, a critical kinase that mediates BCR signaling, is sufficient to suppress IgM plasma cell expansion in Lyn−/− mice, and Ets1 levels are concomitantly restored to normal levels in Btklo Lyn−/− mice (Gutierrez et al., 2010; Luo et al., 2014; Mayeux et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: IgM plasma cell expansion in Lyn-/- mice is driven by exaggerated Btk-dependent BCR stimulation of B2 B cells by endogenous antigens.
source: Therefore, IgM plasma cell expansion in Lyn-/- mice is driven by exaggerated Btk-dependent BCR stimulation of B2 B cells by endogenous antigens (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from cited literature and illustrated in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Enhanced BCR signaling has been shown to favor SLPC fate over GC differentiation in Lyn-sufficient mice as well.
source: Indeed, enhanced BCR signaling has been shown to favor SLPC fate over GC differentiation in Lyn-sufficient mice as well (Chan et al., 2009; Nutt et al., 2015; Paus et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Lyn−/− B cells downregulate Ets1 protein expression.
source: As previously shown, Lyn−/− B cells downregulate Ets1 protein expression (Figure 6A) (Luo et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6A and a citation to prior work.

claim: Lyn-deficient B cells expressing only IgD did not downregulate Ets1, consistent with a reduced ability of IgD to transmit antigen-dependent signals in vivo.
source: However, Lyn-deficient B cells expressing only IgD did not do so, consistent with a reduced ability of IgD to transmit antigen-dependent signals in vivo (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The frequency of plasma cells in the spleens of Lyn−/− mice was increased fourfold relative to Lyn+/+ mice, but the bone marrow plasma cell compartment size was relatively unaffected.
source: As previously reported, we found that the frequency of plasma cells in the spleens of Lyn−/− mice was increased fourfold relative to Lyn+/+ mice, but the bone marrow plasma cell compartment size was relatively unaffected (Figure 6B–C) (Infantino et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6B–C and a citation to prior work.

claim: The increase in splenic plasma cells in Lyn−/− mice was attributable entirely to unswitched (IgM+) plasma cells.
source: The increase in splenic plasma cells was attributable entirely to unswitched (IgM+) plasma cells (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Unswitched plasma cell expansion was completely absent in IgM−/− Lyn−/− spleens.
source: However, unswitched plasma cell expansion was completely absent in IgM−/− Lyn−/− spleens (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: While Lyn−/− mice have elevated serum IgM relative to WT mice, IgM−/− Lyn−/− mice did not have elevated serum IgD relative to IgM−/− mice.
source: This was reflected in steady-state serum antibody levels; while Lyn−/− mice have elevated serum IgM relative to WT mice, IgM−/− Lyn−/− mice did not have elevated serum IgD relative to IgM−/− mice (Figure 6D–E).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 6D–E.

claim: Resistance to unswitched plasma cell expansion is a cell-intrinsic feature of IgD-only Lyn−/− B cells.
source: To confirm that resistance to unswitched plasma cell expansion was a cell-intrinsic feature of IgD-only Lyn−/− B cells, we assessed this phenotype in IgM+/− Lyn−/− mice. Similar to the non-competitive setting, IgD-only Lyn−/− cells did not contribute to an expansion in the unswitched plasma cell compartment (Figure 6F-G).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 6F-G.

claim: The effect of IgD-only cells not contributing to unswitched plasma cell expansion was due to isotype and not VDJ allele usage.
source: This effect was due to isotype and not VDJ allele usage because both IgHa and IgHb B cells in IgHa/b Lyn-/- mice generated unswitched plasma cells in a competitive setting (Figure 5—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3C.

claim: IgD-only Lyn−/− Fo B cells are completely prevented from generating an expanded unswitched SLPC compartment in response to chronic endogenous antigen stimulation, but they are competent to enter the GC.
source: IgD-only Lyn−/− Fo B cells are completely prevented from generating an expanded unswitched SLPC compartment in response to chronic endogenous antigen stimulation, but they are competent to enter the GC.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from data in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Wild type, IgM−/−, and IgD−/− mice all produced extremely robust GC responses 5 days after SRBC injection.
source: We found that wild type, IgM−/−, and IgD−/− mice all produced extremely robust GC responses 5 days after SRBC injection, but B cells expressing IgD alone were unable to produce IgG1+ SLPCs at this time point (Figure 7A–D).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 7A–D.

claim: B cells expressing IgD alone were unable to produce IgG1+ SLPCs 5 days after SRBC injection.
source: We found that wild type, IgM−/−, and IgD−/− mice all produced extremely robust GC responses 5 days after SRBC injection, but B cells expressing IgD alone were unable to produce IgG1+ SLPCs at this time point (Figure 7A–D).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 7A–D.

claim: Both IgD-only and IgM+IgD B cells made a robust contribution to the germinal center response after SRBC immunization.
source: Both cell types made a robust contribution to the germinal center response (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: IgD-only B cells were significantly disfavored in the IgG1+ PC compartment after SRBC immunization, although the defect was less severe than that observed in IgM−/− mice.
source: In contrast to the GC response, IgD-only B cells were significantly disfavored in this compartment, although the defect was less severe than that observed in IgM−/− mice, which lack serum IgM (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: BCR isotypes rather than VDJ locus accounted for differences in IgG1+ PC generation after SRBC immunization.
source: To control for differences in the VDJ locus, we performed this experiment using IgHa/b control mice and observed no significant differences between allotypes, implying that BCR isotypes rather than VDJ locus accounted for our observations (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: IgD-only B cells were able to generate unswitched plasma cells in response to SRBC immunization in both non-competitive and competitive settings.
source: In contrast to impaired IgG1 SLPC responses by IgD-only B cells, we observed that IgD-only B cells were able to generate unswitched plasma cells in response to SRBC immunization in both non-competitive and competitive settings (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C–D.

claim: Unswitched PC numbers correlate well with MZ B cell numbers in IgM−/− and IgD−/− mice.
source: Unswitched PC numbers correlate well with MZ B cell numbers in these mice (Figure 4—figure supplements 1B and Figure 4D).
evidence: This is an observation from data shown in Figure 4—figure supplements 1B and Figure 4D.

claim: MZ B cells efficiently generate short-lived unswitched plasma cells even in response to TD-antigens.
source: Moreover, MZ B cells efficiently generate short-lived unswitched plasma cells even in response to TD-antigens (Phan et al., 2005; Song and Cerny, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: IgG1 PCs emanate from the Fo B cell compartment, while the unswitched PC response may originate in the MZ B cell compartment.
source: We therefore suspect that IgG1 PCs emanate from the Fo B cell compartment, while the unswitched PC response may originate in the MZ B cell compartment.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data.

claim: Normal SLPC generation by IgM-deficient MZ B cells in response to immunization would be consistent with previously reported normal T-independent II responses in IgM-deficient mice.
source: Normal SLPC generation by IgM-deficient MZ B cells in response to immunization would be consistent with previously reported normal T-independent II responses in IgM-deficient mice (Lutz et al., 1998).
evidence: This is an inference supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: GC responses at early time points after NP-RSA immunization were intact in IgD-only cells, but IgG1+ PCs and NP-specific IgG1 titers were significantly reduced 7–8 days after immunization.
source: Although allotype [a] makes a less robust response to NP than allotype [b], we normalized responses of IgD-only cells to wild type allotype [a] cells and found that GC responses at early time points were intact, but IgG1+ PCs and NP-specific IgG1 titers were significantly reduced 7–8 days after immunization (Figure 7G–I).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 7G–I.

claim: IgD-only follicular B cells are competent to enter the GC, but they have defects in adopting the SLPC fate (or class-switching) in response to T-dependent immunization.
source: These data suggest that IgD-only follicular B cells are competent to enter the GC, but they have defects in adopting the SLPC fate (or class-switching) in response to T-dependent immunization.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from data in Figure 7.

claim: The reduced sensitivity of IgD to bona fide endogenous antigen may lie somewhere between complete insensitivity and full sensitivity.
source: Our data suggests that the reduced sensitivity of IgD to bona fide endogenous antigen may lie somewhere between these two extremes; we find that IgD can sense endogenous antigens, just less efficiently than IgM.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Both HEL-specific IgM and IgD BCRs can mediate B cell anergy and drive a common gene expression program in response to chronic high affinity soluble antigen exposure in vivo.
source: Consistent with this conclusion, both HEL-specific IgM and IgD BCRs can mediate B cell anergy and drive a common gene expression program in response to chronic high affinity soluble antigen exposure in vivo (Brink et al., 1992; Sabouri et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: B cells expressing IgD BCR alone inefficiently sense endogenous antigens, and exhibit impaired in vivo cell fate decisions that are dependent upon BCR signal strength.
source: Here we show that B cells expressing IgD BCR alone inefficiently sense endogenous antigens, and exhibit impaired in vivo cell fate decisions that are dependent upon BCR signal strength.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study supported by data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Signal transduction mediated by the IgD BCR in response to anti-Igκ stimulation in vitro is intact for all assayed parameters.
source: Importantly, signal transduction mediated by the IgD BCR in response to anti-Igκ stimulation in vitro is intact for all assayed parameters, suggesting that antigen sensing and signal initiation rather than signal transduction downstream of IgD is impaired.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from data in Figure 2.

claim: Impaired sensing by IgD is conferred by structural properties of IgD, either through direct binding of antigen and signal transduction through the BCR or through differential pairing with co-receptors that directly modulate the BCR signaling pathway.
source: We propose that this impaired sensing is conferred by structural properties of IgD, either through direct binding of antigen and signal transduction through the BCR or through differential pairing with co-receptors that directly modulate the BCR signaling pathway.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal based on the data.

claim: Relevant endogenous antigens may not be exclusively restricted to those that are germline-encoded or generated by host enzymes; rather they may include non-inflammatory antigens taken up through the gastrointestinal tract and recognized by specific BCRs.
source: These antigens may not be exclusively restricted to those that are germline-encoded or generated by host enzymes; rather they may include non-inflammatory antigens taken up through the gastrointestinal tract and recognized by specific BCRs.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the nature of endogenous antigens.

claim: At least some relevant endogenous antigens may be membrane-bound.
source: At least some relevant endogenous antigens may be membrane-bound (Quách et al., 2011; Reed et al., 2016), and recent studies have illustrated the importance of membrane spreading, contraction, and stiffness discrimination in BCR signaling (Fleire et al., 2006; Shaheen et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Relevant endogenous antigens are presented in contexts that do not efficiently trigger signaling through the flexible structure of IgD.
source: We propose that relevant endogenous antigens are presented in contexts that do not efficiently trigger signaling through the flexible structure of IgD.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal based on the data and structural properties of IgD.

claim: Differential clustering of co-receptors with IgD and IgM might influence how BCR signals are integrated in vivo.
source: An alternative mechanism is that differential clustering of co-receptors with IgD and IgM might influence how BCR signals are integrated in vivo.
evidence: This is a speculative alternative mechanism.

claim: IgD is more densely clustered on the cell surface than IgM, and these distinct IgM- and IgD-containing 'islands' are differentially associated with co-receptors such as CD19 in resting and activated B cells.
source: More recently, studies using TIRF, dSTORM, and PLA (proximity ligation assay) showed that IgD is more densely clustered on the cell surface than IgM, and these distinct IgM- and IgD-containing 'islands' are differentially associated with co-receptors such as CD19 in resting and activated B cells (Kläsener et al., 2014; Maity et al., 2015; Mattila et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Differences in cluster density of IgM and IgD might render them differentially sensitive to inhibitory tone from CD22.
source: Since function of the ITIM-containing inhibitory co-receptor CD22 depends on its ability to efficiently access the BCR, differences in cluster density of IgM and IgD might render them differentially sensitive to such inhibitory tone (Gasparrini et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a speculative proposal supported by a citation.

claim: Differential association with co-receptors may contribute to differences in the function of the IgM and IgD BCRs in vivo by modulating BCR signal strength, or by selectively perturbing specific downstream signaling events.
source: It is possible that differential association with such co-receptors contributes to differences in the function of the IgM and IgD BCRs in vivo by modulating BCR signal strength, or by selectively perturbing specific downstream signaling events.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal.

claim: Expression of the IgD BCR is critical for CXCR4-dependent signaling.
source: Becker et al. have shown that expression of the IgD BCR is critical for CXCR4-dependent signaling (Becker et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: CXCR4-deficient B cells exhibit reduced plasma cell migration from spleen to bone marrow (but intact splenic SLPC responses).
source: This may influence the biology of B cells expressing only IgM; indeed, CXCR4-deficient B cells exhibit reduced plasma cell migration from spleen to bone marrow (but intact splenic SLPC responses) (Nie et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: Defective CXCR4 signaling in IgM-only B cells could not account for reduced Nur77-eGFP expression in IgD-only B cells because reporter expression is insensitive to CXCR4 signaling.
source: Importantly, defective CXCR4 signaling in IgM-only B cells could not account for reduced Nur77-eGFP expression in IgD-only B cells because reporter expression is insensitive to CXCR4 signaling (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: B cell responses to TLR4 ligands require expression of the BCR, but canonical TLR ligands do not exhibit selective dependence on either the IgM or the IgD isotypes.
source: B cell responses to TLR4 ligands also require expression of the BCR, but importantly, canonical TLR ligands do not exhibit selective dependence on either the IgM or the IgD isotypes (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: The Fc-receptor for IgM may play a role downstream of serum IgM that is absent in IgM−/− mice.
source: Finally, recent work establishes a role for the Fc-receptor for IgM in modulating B cell responses, and could therefore play a role downstream of serum IgM that is absent in IgM−/− mice (Nguyen et al., 2017a; Nguyen et al., 2017b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: All phenotypes in this study are cell-intrinsic and independent of secreted IgM.
source: We control for this effect by confirming that all phenotypes in this study are cell-intrinsic and independent of secreted IgM.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental design and controls used in the study.

claim: Strong BCR signals favor SLPC over GC fate.
source: Accumulating evidence suggests that strong BCR signals favor SLPC over GC fate (Chan et al., 2009; Nutt et al., 2015; Paus et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Strong BCR signals favoring SLPC fate is thought to be transcriptionally mediated at least in part by loss of Ets1 expression and induction of Irf4 in a BCR signal-strength dependent manner.
source: This is thought to be transcriptionally mediated at least in part by loss of Ets1 expression and induction of Irf4 in a BCR signal-strength dependent manner (Nutt et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: IgM and IgD are each sufficient to drive GC responses, but IgD is less efficient at promoting SLPC fate in response to endogenous antigens.
source: Here we show that IgM and IgD are each sufficient to drive GC responses, but IgD is less efficient at promoting SLPC fate in response to endogenous antigens, implying that IgDhi IgMlo B cells may similarly be shunted away from SLPC responses.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study supported by data in Figures 5, 6, and 7.

claim: The discrepancy between IgM and IgD in promoting SLPC fate is unlikely to be attributable to differences in antigen capture and presentation by the IgM and IgD BCRs, as GC entry is highly T cell-help dependent.
source: This discrepancy is unlikely to be attributable to differences in antigen capture and presentation by the IgM and IgD BCRs, as GC entry is highly T cell-help dependent.
evidence: This is an inference from the data.

claim: In the absence of Lyn, Ets1 downregulation and unswitched PC expansion require the IgM BCR.
source: We show that, in the absence of Lyn, Ets1 downregulation and unswitched PC expansion require the IgM BCR.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 6.

claim: IgM−/−Lyn−/− mice phenocopy BtkloLyn−/− mice; both strains are protected from Ets1-downregulation, PC expansion, and anti-dsDNA autoantibody production in vivo.
source: IgM−/−Lyn−/− mice phenocopy BtkloLyn−/− mice; both strains are protected from Ets1-downregulation, PC expansion, and anti-dsDNA autoantibody production in vivo (Mayeux et al., 2015; Whyburn et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by data in the manuscript and citations to prior work.

claim: Robust Btk-dependent Ets-1 downregulation in response to endogenous antigens relies upon efficient antigen sensing by the IgM BCR and is important to drive unswitched PC expansion in the absence of Lyn.
source: This suggests that robust Btk-dependent Ets-1 downregulation in response to endogenous antigens relies upon efficient antigen sensing by the IgM BCR and is important to drive unswitched PC expansion in the absence of Lyn.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from data in Figure 6 and cited literature.

claim: The purpose (and consequence) of IgM downregulation on autoreactive B cells is to limit their direct differentiation into SLPCs in response to chronic endogenous antigen stimulation, and prevent secretion of auto-antibodies in the context of an acute humoral immune response.
source: We propose that the purpose (and consequence) of IgM downregulation on autoreactive B cells is to limit their direct differentiation into SLPCs in response to chronic endogenous antigen stimulation, and prevent secretion of auto-antibodies in the context of an acute humoral immune response (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: IgD is sufficient to drive germinal center differentiation without the contribution of IgM.
source: However, IgD is sufficient to drive germinal center differentiation without the contribution of IgM. This has been well-demonstrated both in the present study as well as prior work (Lutz et al., 1998).
evidence: This is a conclusion supported by data in the manuscript and a citation to prior work.

claim: Autoreactive IgDhi IgMlo B cells appear to enter the germinal center with greater efficiency, perhaps due in part to improved survival.
source: Indeed, not only are autoreactive IgDhi IgMlo B cells competent to enter the germinal center, they appear to do so with greater efficiency, perhaps due in part to improved survival (Sabouri et al., 2016; Sabouri et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Selection pressures and tolerance mechanisms operating within the germinal center must independently ensure that somatic hypermutation both abolishes germ-line-encoded autoreactivity and prevents de novo acquisition of autoreactivity.
source: It is worth emphasizing that selection pressures and tolerance mechanisms operating within the germinal center must independently ensure that somatic hypermutation both abolishes germ-line-encoded autoreactivity and prevents de novo acquisition of autoreactivity.
evidence: This is a statement about tolerance mechanisms in the germinal center.

claim: Autoreactive BCRs can be 'redeemed' by somatic hypermutation.
source: Goodnow and colleagues recently showed that autoreactive BCRs can indeed be 'redeemed' by somatic hypermutation, providing proof-of-principle that entry of autoreactive B cells into the GC does not necessarily pose a risk to the organism (Sabouri et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: Autoreactive BCRs are retained in the pre-immune B cell compartment to fill holes in the repertoire, and IgD is essential for their survival.
source: One suggestion is that such BCRs are retained in the pre-immune B cell compartment to fill holes in the repertoire, and that IgD is essential for their survival; indeed, it has been shown that loss of IgD expression, with or without compensatory upregulation of IgM, leads to loss of mature naïve B cells in competition (Roes and Rajewsky, 1993; Sabouri et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a speculative proposal supported by citations to prior work.

claim: IgD-only B cells have a profound competitive advantage in the follicular B cell compartment relative to IgM-only (but not WT) B cells, implying an obligate survival function for the IgD isotype BCR.
source: We similarly find that IgD-only B cells have a profound competitive advantage in the follicular B cell compartment relative to IgM-only (but not WT) B cells, implying an obligate survival function for the IgD isotype BCR.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from data in Figure 4.

claim: IgD expression is needed to keep IgMlo B cells alive, which may explain why IgD expression facilitates a broad dynamic range of IgM expression across the B cell repertoire.
source: Since IgD expression is needed to keep IgMlo B cells alive, this may explain why IgD expression facilitates a broad dynamic range of IgM expression across the B cell repertoire (Figure 1B,C), allowing B cells to fine-tune the intensity of their SLPC responses according to their autoreactivity.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data.

claim: IgD expression on IgMlo cells could serve to mediate antigen capture and participation in T-dependent immune responses, while simultaneously limiting SLPC responses.
source: IgD expression on IgMlo cells could serve to mediate antigen capture and participation in T-dependent immune responses, while simultaneously limiting SLPC responses as we show here.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the data.

claim: IgD BCRs sense endogenous antigen more weakly than IgM BCRs in vivo.
source: We demonstrate here for the first time that IgD BCRs sense endogenous antigen more weakly than IgM BCRs in vivo, are inefficient at driving SLPC responses to endogenous antigens, and thereby may function to divert autoreactive follicular B cells from direct PC differentiation.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study supported by data throughout the manuscript.

claim: The property of the IgD BCR to sense endogenous antigen more weakly limits generation of auto-reactive antibodies in the context of immediate humoral immune responses.
source: We propose that this property of the IgD BCR limits generation of auto-reactive antibodies in the context of immediate humoral immune responses.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the data.

claim: IgM downregulation in the face of high IgD expression regulates the fate of naïve autoreactive B cells in vivo while retaining their contribution to the mature BCR repertoire.
source: Taken together with recent work from the Jumaa and Goodnow groups, we propose a unified model of how IgM downregulation in the face of high IgD expression regulates the fate of naïve autoreactive B cells in vivo while retaining their contribution to the mature BCR repertoire.
evidence: This is a proposed unified model based on the data and prior work.
